web_evidence.title: University of Strathclyde thesis, Chapter 3: Performing Femininity in Invitation to the Waltz
web_evidence.note: Scholarly structural analysis describes the novel as internally focalized on Olivia and largely presented through free-indirect speech, with Olivia's thoughts only occasionally rendered directly; this accounts for local first-person thought within third-person narration.

web_evidence.title: Invitation to the Waltz — Rosamond Lehmann: excerpts
web_evidence.note: Sustained excerpts from chapters 14, 20, and 21 repeatedly narrate Olivia as 'she' while embedding brief first-person thoughts, demonstrating the interior narrative pattern.

web_evidence.title: Invitation to the Waltz — Shelf Love
web_evidence.note: The reviewer explicitly identifies a third-person narrative whose focal attention shifts between Olivia and Kate, with Olivia primary.

web_evidence.title: Invitation to the Waltz by Rosamond Lehmann | Hachette UK
web_evidence.note: The publisher's description identifies the diary as a gift Olivia receives for her seventeenth birthday, corroborating that the journal material is embedded rather than the novel's constitutive narrative form.

person_note: The controlling narration is third person, principally internally focalized through Olivia and at times through Kate. Quote q00005 directly shows the narrator naming Olivia and reporting her actions before entering free-indirect thought, and both the scholarly analysis and sustained interior excerpts confirm that this is the novel's general method. The first-person passages are Olivia's direct thoughts or entries in the diary she receives as a birthday gift; they are local embedded voices, not sustained autonomous narration. No credible evidence indicates a first-person base section or an alternating-person structure.
